title: What is known about 1RB1LA_1LC0RE_1LF1LD_0RB0LA_1RC1RE_---0LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_1LC0RE_1LF1LD_0RB0LA_1RC1RE_---0LD.
intro: This is Space Needle, a six-state machine found by mxdys in January 2025 and listed by the bbchallenge community as a cryptid: its halting from blank tape is equivalent to an open number-theory question. This page records what is established here, sorted by what each result rests on.

The tape is a few long blocks of 1s. From one visit of the left edge to the next, the machine applies mxdys's map to the lengths (b, c) of the two blocks of 0^∞ A>0 1^b 0 0 1^c 0^∞. Lean proves the map, for all b and c, and proves that the machine halts exactly when Katelyn Doucette's one-variable sequence 6, 10, 17, 41, 101, 251, ... reaches a power of two.
verdict: The question is open, and equivalent to a question about a simple sequence. Lean proves, checked by the kernel alone, that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if some term of the sequence D0 = 6, Dk+1 = Dk + v + 3a, where Dk = 2v(2a+1), is a power of two (halts_iff_pow2).

None of the first 300,000 terms is (Lean, native_decide; the first 20,000 by the kernel), nor of the first 3·106 (C). The terms grow by a factor of about 1.92 per step and their number of factors 2 stays small (at most 24 so far), so a power of two would be an extraordinary coincidence: the machine is probviously non-halting. A proof would need control of the 2-adic valuations of a sequence defined by additions, which is beyond current methods.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when F reads a 0.

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: Fifteen rules on symbolic tapes, for all values of their parameters and any surrounding tape: one bounce of the bouncer (L 0 1^(m+3) C>0 R to L 1 0 1^(m+1) C>0 1 R), one zig-zag, the ends of the phases, the halt of (1, c), and blank tape to (3, 1) in 45 steps. Written by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py as chains of rfl steps and the crossing lemmas.

claims.title: mxdys's macro rules
claims.text: Write X(b, c) for 0^∞ A>0 1^b 0 0 1^c 0^∞. For every b and c ≥ 1: X(0, c) reaches X(c + 2, 1); X(2k + 2, c) reaches X(5k + c + 7, 1); X(2k + 3, c) reaches X(k, k + c + 4); X(1, c) halts 13 steps later. Proved by three inductions (the bouncer, the zig-zag, the shift of a block) over the shift rules.

claims.title: The reduction to mxdys's map
claims.text: Let g be the map above on pairs (b, c), and orbit n its n-th iterate from (3, 1). The machine halts from blank tape if and only if some orbit n has b = 1.

claims.title: The reduction to Doucette's sequence
claims.text: Let D<sub>0</sub> = 6 and D<sub>k+1</sub> = F(D<sub>k</sub>) with F(D) = D + v + 3a for D = 2<sup>v</sup>(2a + 1). The configurations X(b, 1) of the orbit are exactly b = D<sub>k</sub> − 3; between two of them come v odd steps, each halving b + 3, and one even step. So the machine halts from blank tape if and only if some D<sub>k</sub> is a power of two.

claims.title: No power of two in the first 20,000 terms
claims.text: Checked by the kernel's arithmetic (numbers up to about 19,000 bits). By the reduction, no halt before the machine's 20,000th visit to a configuration X(b, 1).

claims.title: No power of two in the first 300,000 terms
claims.text: The same check by compiled code (numbers up to about 282,000 bits).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: Direct run of the list simulator from blank tape.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run by compiled code.

claims.title: The macro rules against the machine
claims.text: A direct run of 3·1010 steps (c/verify.c) meets the shape X(b, c) exactly at the configurations the orbit of g predicts, in order, and at no others: 19 of them, from X(3, 1) at step 45 to X(7483, 1) at step 10,608,569,291 and X(3740, 3745) at step 10,636,589,390.

claims.title: No power of two in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> terms
claims.text: Multi-precision C (c/doucette.c, checked against Python for the first 105 terms: bit length and largest v agree). The 3·106th term has about 2.8·106 bits; the largest v seen is 24, the mean v is 0.998. The community reports 108 terms with at most 25 factors of 2.

claims.title: Probviously non-halting
claims.text: If the low bits of D<sub>k</sub> behave like random bits, v is geometric with mean 1, D grows by an average factor of about 1.920 per term (0.9412 bits, LegionMammal978's estimate; 0.9414 measured), and the chance that a term of n bits is a power of two is about 2<sup>−n</sup>. Summed over the terms after the ones checked, the chance of a halt is far below 10<sup>−10000</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Equivalent (in Lean) to: does Doucette's sequence ever reach a power of two? No method is known that controls the 2-adic valuation of terms of such a sequence.

explainer.lede: Space Needle is one of the community's cryptids: whether it halts is equivalent to whether a simple sequence of numbers, 6, 10, 17, 41, 101, 251, 626, ..., ever reaches a power of two. This page shows how the machine computes that sequence, and what is proved about it.

facts.text: Lean: halts from blank tape iff Doucette's sequence hits a power of two.
None of them a power of two (Lean); 20,000 by the kernel alone.
None of them a power of two (C); at most 24 factors of 2.
The terms grow by ×1.92 each; hitting 2<sup>n</sup> exactly is a vanishing coincidence.

sections.heading: Blocks of 1s, and a state that keeps coming back
html: Run the simulator to step 45 and the tape reads A>0 1 1 1 0 0 1: the head, in state A, on the 0 just left of everything, then a block of three 1s, a gap of two 0s, a block of one 1. Call this shape
X(b, c) = 0^∞ A>0 1^b 0 0 1^c 0^∞

so step 45 is X(3, 1). The machine keeps coming back to this shape: X(0, 5) at step 64, X(7, 1) at 107, X(2, 7) at 158, X(14, 1) at 274, X(38, 1) at 2,640, X(98, 1) at 31,346, X(248, 1) at 434,602. In between, the tape holds two or three long blocks of 1s separated by single 0s, and the head works on them in long regular phases. Nothing else ever happens: the whole run is these visits and the phases between them.

sections.heading: Bouncer, zig-zag, shift
html: Take X(14, 1). Three kinds of motion carry it to X(38, 1):

• The bouncer. A writes a 1 left of the block and the head runs to the right end of the block. From 0 1^(m+3) C>0, states C, F, D erase two 1s, A runs left, B and E run right: the middle block loses two 1s and each side gains one, 1 0 1^(m+1) C>0 1. Repeated, the block of 14 shrinks to 2 while blocks of 7 grow on both sides. Each bounce crosses the whole block, so this phase takes time quadratic in b.

• The zig-zag. Then the head stands at the left end in state A, before 1^a 0 1^b. Going back and forth it moves the 0 between the two blocks one cell at a time, ending with the first block one shorter, the second two longer, and the whole picture one cell further left: A>0 1^(a+1) 0 1^b becomes A>0 1^a 0 1^(b+2). Repeated a times, the first block disappears into the second.
• The merges. When the first block is empty, the gap of two 0s closes up and the next block becomes the first; with no block left after it, the tape is X(m, 1) again.

For X(14, 1): the bouncer leaves 1^7 0 1^2 C>0 1^7, then A>0 1^6 0 1^2 0 1^8; six zig-zags give A>0 0 1^14 0 1^8; a merge gives A>0 1^15 0 1^8; fifteen zig-zags give A>0 0 1^38, and the last merge X(38, 1). Each of these steps is a lemma in Lean, proved for all values of the lengths.

sections.heading: mxdys's rules
html: Done in general, the phases give one rule per case of b:

fromtowhat happens
X(0, c)X(c + 2, 1)the empty block merges
X(1, c)halt13 steps later F reads a 0
X(2k + 2, c)X(5k + c + 7, 1)bouncer, k zig-zags, merge, 2k + 3 zig-zags, merge
X(2k + 3, c)X(k, k + c + 4)bouncer ends on an odd block: b roughly halves

An even b multiplies b by about 5/2 and resets c to 1; an odd b halves b and stores the rest in c. The machine halts when b reaches 1, which can only happen by halving. Lean proves the four rules and that the machine halts from blank tape exactly when the orbit of (3, 1) reaches b = 1 (halts_iff in lean/Macro.lean).

sections.heading: Doucette's sequence
html: Look only at the visits X(b, 1) and write D = b + 3. Between two of them, the odd rule applies v times, where 2v is the largest power of two dividing D: each odd step halves D exactly (b + 3 becomes (b + 3)/2) and adds to c. Then one even step uses everything stored in c. Adding it up, the next D is
F(D) = D + v + 3a,   where D = 2^v · (2a + 1).

From X(3, 1), D = 6, and the sequence runs 6, 10, 17, 41, 101, 251, 626, 1095, 2736, 2995, 7486, 13100, … If some D is a power of two, the halvings run down to D = 4, which is b = 1: the machine halts. If not, they always stop at an odd D ≥ 3 and the even step follows. Lean proves this equivalence (halts_iff_pow2 in lean/Collatz.lean): Space Needle halts if and only if Doucette's sequence reaches a power of two.

Each term is a visit to the left edge, and each costs far more machine steps than the last (a cubic number in b): the visit X(2992, 1) (D = 2995) comes at step 519,524,312, the next one, X(7483, 1), at step 10,608,569,291. The sequence itself is cheap: Lean's kernel checks the first 20,000 terms, compiled Lean 300,000, and C 3·106. None is a power of two.

sections.heading: A coincidence that should never happen
html: F(D) is about D · (1 + 3/2v+1): an odd D grows by a factor of about 5/2, a D with many factors 2 by much less. If the low bits of the terms are like random bits, v is 0 half the time, 1 a quarter of the time, and so on, and D gains about 0.94 bits per step (a factor of 1.92). A number of n bits is a power of two with chance about 2−n, so the chance that any term after the first few dozen is a power of two is astronomically small. In 3·106 terms, v has never exceeded 24.

So the machine almost certainly never halts. Proving it is another matter: one would have to show that a sequence built by additions never has all its bits but one equal to 0, that is, control the 2-adic valuation of every term. Questions of this kind (like the Collatz problem) are beyond present mathematics, which is why Space Needle is called a cryptid. Run backwards, the condition is a chain of congruences: a power of two 2n can be reached from a multiple of 2k only for special n (for k = 0, only n ≡ 0 mod 4), and the smallest powers of two reachable within a few steps are already enormous; but no one has turned this into a proof.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.311). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.059).
After 109 steps the tape spans 3,249 cells (2,978 left of the start, 23 right), with a density of 1s of 0.999.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

family: Collatz-like map on block lengths (2-adic valuation map)
summary: Space Needle: halts iff Doucette's sequence 6, 10, 17, 41, 101, ... (D -> D + v + 3a for D = 2^v(2a+1)) hits a power of two; proved equivalent in Lean, probviously non-halting.
